docs.title: Trade Surveillance Agent
docs.text:
Insider-trading surveillance that has to show its work.

In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

This system reads a securities transaction reported to the SEC and investigates whether it looks like insider trading. It only concludes something once every claim in its report is backed by a specific piece of retrieved evidence — and it says so when it isn't sure.

Status: in development. This site is being built alongside the code, phase by phase — see the build plan for what exists today.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Takes a securities transaction in SEC Form 4 shape and runs an investigation: it pulls the transaction record, checks the insider's applicable trading limits, retrieves compliance rules with severity tiers, computes trading volume against thresholds, and compares against the insider's own history. It issues a finding — clear / flag / escalate — where every assertion traces to a retrieved fact.

docs.title: The centrepiece: a grounding judge that rejects its own draft
docs.text: Most systems like this write a conclusion and hope it is supported. This one writes a draft, decomposes it into individual claims, checks every claim against the evidence actually retrieved, and — if anything is unsupported — sends the investigation back for another evidence pass. Only a fully grounded draft is ever published, and the published finding is guaranteed to be byte-identical to the one that passed the check. See Grounding.

docs.text: Severity Finding Status High POST /investigations returned 202 for an accession that is not in facts.db; the run then failed in a background task. Fixed: the route looks the accession up first and returns 404 with an actionable detail, creating no run. The UI shows the message. High The API had no CORS policy, so a browser page on localhost:3000 calling the API on :8000 was blocked. Fixed: SURVEILLANCE_FRONTEND_ORIGINS allow-list; development also trusts any localhost port, other environments do not. High No production compose file, frontend image, .dockerignore or deployment guide. Added compose.prod.yaml, frontend/Dockerfile (standalone Next.js build, non-root, health check), both .dockerignore files and Deploy to a server. Images not yet built here (no Docker in the authoring environment). Medium The API image did not trust the proxy's X-Forwarded-For, so the per-client rate limit would have seen one address, the proxy's, for every visitor. Fixed: --proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips "*", safe only because no host port is published and the proxy overwrites the header (documented in the deploy guide). Medium A run in flight at a restart stayed running forever. Fixed: on startup the API marks such runs failed ("interrupted by a server restart"). Medium No authentication, and every investigation spends model credits. Not fixed in the app by design; the deploy guide puts basic auth at the proxy. The rate limit is a backstop. Low Two POSTs for the same accession start two independent runs. Accepted. Runs are replayable records, the rate limit bounds the cost, and the run id (not the accession) is the key. An atomic claim would only matter if a run mutated shared state. Low docs/PLAN.md refers to docs/regulatory_basis.md; the file is docs/regulatory-basis.md. Noted. Low docs/PLAN.md §11 says every chart regenerates byte-identically, but CI has no such check and the SVGs embed run-specific data (latency, metadata), so regenerating them changes the files. Open. Only the RL results JSON, which is deterministic, has a CI drift check. Low The API's finding field is opaque JSON in the OpenAPI document, so generated types do not describe it. Accepted. frontend/src/lib/schemas.ts validates it at runtime and is the frontend's source of truth.

docs.title: Found by the live run
docs.text: Severity Finding High Every real investigation through the API failed: LangGraph's default recursion limit of 25 is below a real run's length (about two steps per tool call, plus two evidence passes). Tests passed because the eval harness set its own limit of 100 and the API tests use fake chains. Medium With real models the claim extractor cited no tool-call ids in 5 of 10 runs (provider ids such as call_... are long and opaque), so those findings scored 0 on the process audit's citation check. The audit worked as designed; the extractor is the weak point. Candidate fix: give the extractor short ids (t1, t2, ...) that map back to the real ones. Medium After the two evidence passes, findings are published even when the judge still marks claims unsupported (1 to 5 per run here). The count is shown, but a reader can miss it. Candidate fix: label such findings as partially grounded in the UI.

docs.title: Failure visibility
docs.text: A background failure reaches the UI as a run error: RunConsole renders the stored error when a run ends failed, and the API now also fails runs cut off by a restart instead of leaving them running.

docs.text: The components/ui/ primitives are copied from clinical_care_navigator rather than shared, which makes this the third copy of them. Extraction into a shared @zarreh/agent-ui package is portfolio decision D20 (PORTFOLIO_PLAN_V4.md §15), planned for after this app's UI phase.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
API-contract request/response models — separate from schemas/, which holds the domain models the graph itself produces (docs/PLAN.md §5.2).

Runs one investigation to completion, persisting every node event and the final finding to the RunStore as it happens — so a run is replayable from the store whether a client is watching live or reconnects later (docs/PLAN.md §7 Phase 5). Runs as an in-process background task: a single-instance demo deployment doesn't need a separate task queue (same reasoning as SQLite over Postgres for this phase, docs/PLAN.md §5.2).

Read-write repository over runs.db — the operational record of every investigation, persisted so a run is replayable from the store at any time, during execution or long after it finished (docs/PLAN.md §7 Phase 5).

Unlike FactStore/PolicyStore, this store creates its own schema on first use: it holds operational state, not build-time data.

Per-node LLM cost accounting via a LangChain callback (docs/PLAN.md §5.5).

Implemented in zarreh_agentkit.cost (extracted substrate); re-exported here so surveillance.graph.cost_tracking imports keep working. The price table there covers this app's models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o).

def cors_options(config: Settings) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Configured origins only; development also trusts any localhost port,
    because `next dev` moves to :3001 when :3000 is taken."""
    options: dict[str, object] = {
        "allow_origins": config.frontend_origins,
        "allow_methods": ["GET", "POST"],
        "allow_headers": ["Content-Type"],
    }
    if config.environment == "development":
        options["allow_origin_regex"] = _LOCALHOST_ORIGIN
    return options

docs.title: create_investigation(request, body, background_tasks, graph, run_store, fact_store, settings) async
docs.text:
Starts one investigation as a background task and returns immediately — poll GET /{id} or stream GET /{id}/events for progress. Two POSTs for the same accession start two independent runs (see docs/HARVEST.md).

Source code in src/surveillance/api/routes/investigations.py 
@router.post("", status_code=202)
@limiter.limit(DEFAULT_RATE_LIMIT)
async def create_investigation(
    request: Request,
    body: CreateInvestigationRequest,
    background_tasks: BackgroundTasks,
    graph: SurveillanceGraphDep,
    run_store: RunStoreDep,
    fact_store: FactStoreDep,
    settings: SettingsDep,
) -> CreateInvestigationResponse:
    """Starts one investigation as a background task and returns immediately
    — poll `GET /{id}` or stream `GET /{id}/events` for progress. Two POSTs
    for the same accession start two independent runs (see docs/HARVEST.md)."""
    if fact_store.get_transaction(body.accession_number) is None:
        raise HTTPException(
            status_code=404,
            detail=(
                f"Accession {body.accession_number!r} is not in the facts database. "
                "Use an accession number from the loaded Form 4 filings."
            ),
        )
    run_id = str(uuid4())
    run_store.create_run(run_id, body.accession_number)
    background_tasks.add_task(
        execute_investigation, run_id, body.accession_number, graph, run_store, settings
    )
    return CreateInvestigationResponse(id=run_id, status="running")

docs.title: WithRecursionLimit
docs.text:
astream_events ignores a limit bound with with_config, and the shared run executor offers no way to pass one, so the limit is injected per call here.

Source code in src/surveillance/api/run_executor.py 
class WithRecursionLimit:
    """`astream_events` ignores a limit bound with `with_config`, and the shared run
    executor offers no way to pass one, so the limit is injected per call here."""

    def __init__(self, graph: Any, limit: int = RECURSION_LIMIT) -> None:
        self._graph = graph
        self._limit = limit

    def astream_events(self, graph_input: Any, config: Any = None, **kwargs: Any) -> Any:
        merged = {**(config or {}), "recursion_limit": self._limit}
        return self._graph.astream_events(graph_input, config=merged, **kwargs)

docs.title: RunStore
docs.text:
Bases: RunEventLog

Persists investigation runs, their node-by-node events, and per-node LLM cost — the single source of truth GET /investigations/{id} and GET /investigations/{id}/events read from. Events and costs come from zarreh_agentkit.runs.RunEventLog; the runs table is this app's own.

Source code in src/surveillance/store/run_store.py 
class RunStore(RunEventLog):
    """Persists investigation runs, their node-by-node events, and per-node
    LLM cost — the single source of truth `GET /investigations/{id}` and
    `GET /investigations/{id}/events` read from. Events and costs come from
    `zarreh_agentkit.runs.RunEventLog`; the `runs` table is this app's own."""

    def __init__(self, db_path: Path) -> None:
        super().__init__(db_path)
        self._conn.executescript(_SCHEMA)
        self._conn.commit()

    def create_run(self, run_id: str, accession_number: str) -> None:
        now = utc_now()
        self._conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO runs (id, accession_number, status, created_at, updated_at) "
            "VALUES (?, ?, 'running', ?, ?)",
            (run_id, accession_number, now, now),
        )
        self._conn.commit()

    def get_run(self, run_id: str) -> RunRecord | None:
        row = self._conn.execute(
            "SELECT id, accession_number, status, created_at, updated_at, "
            "finding_kind, finding_json, error FROM runs WHERE id = ?",
            (run_id,),
        ).fetchone()
        return _run_from_row(row) if row else None

    def complete_run(self, run_id: str, finding_kind: str, finding_json: str) -> None:
        self._conn.execute(
            "UPDATE runs SET status = 'completed', updated_at = ?, "
            "finding_kind = ?, finding_json = ? WHERE id = ?",
            (utc_now(), finding_kind, finding_json, run_id),
        )
        self._conn.commit()

    def fail_run(self, run_id: str, error: str) -> None:
        self._conn.execute(
            "UPDATE runs SET status = 'failed', updated_at = ?, error = ? WHERE id = ?",
            (utc_now(), error, run_id),
        )
        self._conn.commit()

    def fail_interrupted_runs(self, reason: str) -> int:
        """Runs execute in-process, so any run still `running` at startup was
        cut off by a restart and can never finish."""
        cursor = self._conn.execute(
            "UPDATE runs SET status = 'failed', updated_at = ?, error = ? WHERE status = 'running'",
            (utc_now(), reason),
        )
        self._conn.commit()
        return cursor.rowcount

docs.title: Deploy to a server
docs.text:
How to run the Trade Surveillance Agent on a Linux server behind HTTPS, using compose.prod.yaml. It builds the API and the web app and publishes no host ports: a reverse proxy is the only way in.

The browser talks to one origin. The proxy sends /api/* to the API (removing the /api prefix, because the API itself has no such prefix) and everything else to the web app.

Not yet exercised end to end

The steps are adapted from a deployment that was verified for a sibling app. For this repository the compose file and both Dockerfiles have been written and the API behaviour they rely on is tested, but the images have not been built or run behind a proxy yet, and HTTPS certificates and DNS have not been exercised.

docs.title: 1. What you need
docs.text:
• A Linux server with a public IP, reachable by SSH.
  • A domain name with an A record pointing at the server (for example surveillance.example.com).
  • Docker Engine with the Compose plugin (docker compose version should work).
  • An OpenAI API key.
  • Ports 80 and 443 open to the internet, and nothing else except SSH.

docs.title: 2. Get the code onto the server
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/zarreh/trade_sureillance_agent.git
cd trade_sureillance_agent

The continuous-deployment workflow publishes the API image to GitHub Container Registry but not the web image, and its server-deploy job is still a placeholder. So this guide builds both images on the server.

docs.title: 3. Put the data on the server
docs.text:
The API reads two read-only databases from data/ (facts.db, policy.db) and writes one of its own there at runtime (runs.db). data/ is git-ignored and excluded from the image, so you have to provide it. Pick one option.

=== "Build it on the server"

Needs [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and outbound internet access (it
downloads SEC EDGAR bulk files; see [Data pipeline](architecture/data-pipeline.md)).

```bash
uv sync --extra dev
make data
```

=== "Build it locally and copy it"

On the machine where you already ran `make data`, copy **only** the two
read-only databases:

```bash
rsync -av \
  --include='facts.db' --include='policy.db' \
  --exclude='*' \
  data/ you@your-server:~/trade_sureillance_agent/data/
```

Do not copy `runs.db`: it is the other machine's run history.

The API container runs as user 1000, so that user must be able to write to data/:

sudo chown -R 1000:1000 data

Without this the API exits at startup with sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file.

docs.title: 4. Configure
docs.text:
Create .env in the repository root. It is read by docker compose for the API container, and the two WEB_PUBLIC_* lines are also used as build arguments for the web image.

# --- API (runtime) ---
SURVEILLANCE_OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
SURVEILLANCE_ENVIRONMENT=production
SURVEILLANCE_FRONTEND_ORIGINS='["https://surveillance.example.com"]'

# --- Web (baked into the JavaScript at build time) ---
WEB_PUBLIC_API_URL=https://surveillance.example.com/api
WEB_PUBLIC_DOCS_URL=https://zarreh.github.io/trade_sureillance_agent/
Variable Why it matters SURVEILLANCE_OPENAI_API_KEY Without it, runs that need the model fail. SURVEILLANCE_ENVIRONMENT Anything other than development switches logs to JSON and stops trusting localhost origins. SURVEILLANCE_FRONTEND_ORIGINS CORS allow-list as a JSON list. Outside development this is the only thing trusted. Because the proxy serves the site and the API from one origin the browser does not need CORS, but set it to your public origin anyway. WEB_PUBLIC_API_URL Where the browser calls the API. Must be the public URL ending in /api. The default, http://localhost/api, only works on the server itself. WEB_PUBLIC_DOCS_URL Target of the Docs links. Point it at wherever the documentation site is published.

Optional: SURVEILLANCE_LANGSMITH_API_KEY for tracing, SURVEILLANCE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE, SURVEILLANCE_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES.

The two WEB_PUBLIC_* values are build-time

Next.js inlines them into the bundle. Changing them in .env does nothing until you rebuild the web image (docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml up -d --build). A site whose API calls go to localhost was built without WEB_PUBLIC_API_URL.

Keep .env out of git

It holds your API key. It is already git-ignored and excluded from the images.

docs.title: 5. Set up the reverse proxy
docs.text:
compose.prod.yaml attaches both services to an external Docker network named edge. Create it once, then run a proxy on it. The services are named surveillance-api and surveillance-web so they don't clash with other apps sharing the network.

docker network create edge     # skip if it already exists

~/proxy/compose.yaml:

services:
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy_data:/data        # certificates live here
      - caddy_config:/config
    networks:
      - edge

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:

networks:
  edge:
    external: true

~/proxy/Caddyfile:

surveillance.example.com {
        handle_path /api/* {
                reverse_proxy surveillance-api:8000 {
                        flush_interval -1
                }
        }

        handle {
                encode zstd gzip
                reverse_proxy surveillance-web:3000
        }
}
  • handle_path strips /api before forwarding. Without it the API sees /api/investigations and returns 404.
  • flush_interval -1 sends the live run stream through immediately instead of buffering it, and encode is deliberately kept off the /api routes so the stream is never compressed into a lump.

Caddy also requests and renews the HTTPS certificate by itself.

nginx instead of Caddy 
location /api/ {
    proxy_pass http://surveillance-api:8000/;   # trailing slash strips /api
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_buffering off;                        # server-sent events
    proxy_read_timeout 120s;
}
location / {
    proxy_pass http://surveillance-web:3000;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
}

docs.title: 6. Start the app
docs.text:
docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml up -d --build
docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml ps          # both should say "healthy"
curl https://surveillance.example.com/api/healthz

The web container waits for the API's health check before it starts. Open the site and confirm an investigation streams node by node and ends in a finding.

docs.title: 7. Protect the site
docs.text:
Do this before the site is public

The app has no login, and every investigation spends your model credits. The per-client rate limit is a backstop, not access control. Put basic auth at the proxy; because the page and its API calls share one origin, one rule covers both.

docker compose -f ~/proxy/compose.yaml exec caddy caddy hash-password

surveillance.example.com {
        basic_auth {
                reviewer <paste-the-hash-here>
        }

        handle_path /api/* {
                # ...unchanged...
        }
        handle {
                # ...unchanged...
        }
}

To keep the home page public and protect only the paid endpoint, scope the rule to @start method POST and path /api/investigations. Do not put an API key in browser code: anything in the browser is visible to everyone.

docs.title: 8. Operate it
docs.text:
Logs

docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml logs -f surveillance-api

Update to a new version

git pull
docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml up -d --build

data/ is untouched. A run in flight during the restart cannot finish; on startup the API marks it failed ("interrupted by a server restart") so the page shows an error instead of waiting forever.

Back up

facts.db and policy.db are rebuildable with make data. Only runs.db is unique to the server:

mkdir -p backups
sqlite3 data/runs.db ".backup 'backups/runs-$(date +%F).db'"

Run one API process. Runs execute inside the API process and the store is a SQLite file, so do not scale surveillance-api to several replicas or workers.

Duplicate starts. Two POST /investigations calls for the same accession start two independent runs. That is allowed on purpose: runs are replayable records, and the rate limit bounds the cost.

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause and fix API container exits with unable to open database file data/ is not writable by user 1000. Run sudo chown -R 1000:1000 data. The page loads but every start fails, or the browser tries localhost WEB_PUBLIC_API_URL was missing or wrong when the web image was built. Fix .env and rebuild with up -d --build. 404 on every API call through the proxy The proxy is not stripping /api. Use handle_path (Caddy) or a trailing slash on proxy_pass (nginx). The run seems to hang, then everything appears at once The proxy is buffering the event stream. Use flush_interval -1 (Caddy) or proxy_buffering off (nginx), and do not compress /api. "Accession … is not in the facts database" The accession is not in data/facts.db. Use one from the loaded filings, or rebuild the data. The browser blocks the call (CORS error) The page's origin is not in SURVEILLANCE_FRONTEND_ORIGINS. Add the exact public origin (scheme and host, no path) and restart the API. Everyone gets 429 Too many requests The rate limit is per client address. If the proxy does not pass the real client address, all visitors share one bucket. Make the proxy set X-Forwarded-For (Caddy does by default). Runs fail with an authentication error from the model SURVEILLANCE_OPENAI_API_KEY is missing or wrong. Fix .env, then docker compose -f compose.prod.yaml up -d.

docs.title: 10. Security notes
docs.text:
• The API trusts X-Forwarded-For from any peer (--forwarded-allow-ips "*") so the per-client rate limit sees real visitors. That is safe only because no host port is published and the proxy replaces the header. Never publish the API port directly.
  • Open only 22, 80 and 443 in the server firewall.
  • The trade data is public SEC filings, but the role limits, compliance rules and corporate-events calendar are synthetic. The app is a research prototype, not a supervisory system of record.

docs.title: Regulatory basis
docs.text:
This is a research prototype, not legal or compliance advice

Nothing on this page or produced by this system has been reviewed by a licensed attorney or compliance professional. It is a portfolio engineering project demonstrating a grounded-AI architecture over a realistic regulatory domain — not a system of record, not investment or legal advice, and not a substitute for a firm's actual compliance program. Every rule, threshold, and role limit this system applies (except where explicitly cited below) is synthetic data invented for this project. Do not rely on any output of this system for a real compliance decision.

docs.title: What this system actually investigates
docs.text:
This system reasons over SEC Form 4 filings — reports of changes in beneficial ownership that officers, directors, and beneficial owners of more than 10% of a registered class of equity securities must file under Section 16(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. § 78p(a)). Since the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, Section 16(a) generally requires these transactions to be reported within two business days of the transaction. filing_lag_trading_days (data/build_store.py) measures exactly this gap, computed against the NYSE trading calendar (pandas-market-calendars, data/dates.py::nyse_trading_days_between) — business-day counting must use the calendar the exchanges actually observe, not a generic weekday count, since the two differ around exchange holidays. This is this repository's implementation choice of calendar source, not itself a citation to a specific rule text.

SEC Rule 10b-5 (17 CFR § 240.10b-5), adopted under Section 10(b) of the Exchange Act, is the general anti-fraud provision most insider-trading enforcement is built on — it prohibits fraud and deception in connection with the purchase or sale of any security, including trading on material nonpublic information. This system does not implement Rule 10b-5 itself; it implements a surveillance heuristic (transaction value against a role limit, timing against a seeded corporate-events calendar, rolling volume against the insider's own history) that a human compliance reviewer would use as a starting point for the kind of inquiry Rule 10b-5 concerns.

docs.title: Rule 10b5-1 as a reported, not verified, signal
docs.text: Rule 10b5-1 (17 CFR § 240.10b5-1) provides an affirmative defense against insider-trading liability for trades made under a written trading plan adopted in good faith, before the person was aware of material nonpublic information, and (following the SEC's 2022 amendments) subject to a cooling-off period and related conditions. This system's reported_under_10b5_1 field (tri-state: true / false / unknown, store/models.py::Transaction) reflects only whether the filing itself reported the indicator — never whether a plan was independently verified against these conditions. unknown is rendered everywhere in this system, including the UI, as "not established", never as an absence of a plan (D-A2-5) — the distinction matters because a plan can be real and simply not captured by this field's encoding (SEC's own bulk data shows the field encoded inconsistently across filers, docs/PLAN.md §4.3).

docs.title: Why a human reviewer stays in the loop
docs.text: FINRA Rule 3110 requires broker-dealers to establish and maintain a system to supervise the activities of their associated persons, including review of the kinds of transactions this system investigates. This system does not implement or replace that supervisory obligation — it is not a broker-dealer's compliance system, has not been reviewed by one, and every finding it produces is a research artifact for a human reviewer, never a supervisory determination on its own (docs/how-it-works/what-it-wont-do.md). Rule 3110 is cited here as the reason a system like this belongs inside a supervised compliance workflow with a human decision-maker, not as a claim that this prototype satisfies it.

docs.title: What is synthetic
docs.text:
• Role-based trading limits (role_limits table, data/generate_compliance_db.py::ROLE_LIMITS) — invented thresholds by relationship and authorization level, not any real firm's policy.
  • Compliance rule table (compliance_rules, data/generate_compliance_db.py::COMPLIANCE_RULES) — a synthetic severity-tiered rule table, not a real firm's rule book or SEC rule text.
  • Corporate-events calendar (material_events, seeded per issuer with a fixed random seed) — a synthetic earnings calendar and blackout window, not any real company's actual event dates.
  • The transaction data itself is real: fetched from SEC EDGAR's bulk Insider Transactions Data Sets (data/fetch_edgar.py), which is public domain. See docs/evidence/data-profile.md for known data-quality limitations in that source (approximately 0.4% of dates show filer-entered typos, e.g. a four-digit year off by one — SEC's own bulk data disclaims this).

docs.title: Scope this system does not claim
docs.text: See What it won't do for the complete list. In summary: it does not watch live trades or price feeds, it does not decide anything on its own, and it is not investment, legal, or compliance advice.

make data

Fetches SEC EDGAR bulk data, builds the local fact and policy stores, and seeds the labelled scenarios. See docs/PLAN.md §4 for what this does and why.

docs.title: Investigating a filing
docs.text:
curl -sX POST localhost:8000/investigations \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"accession_number": "0000000001-25-000001"}'
# {"id": "…", "status": "running"}

curl -s localhost:8000/investigations/<id>
curl -sN localhost:8000/investigations/<id>/events   # SSE, node-by-node

GET /investigations/{id}/events replays every persisted node event from the start and then tails new ones until the run finishes — reconnecting later just replays from RunStore (data/runs.db), no run is lost. Requests are rate-limited (SURVEILLANCE_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE, default 20/minute) and request bodies are capped (SURVEILLANCE_MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES, default 16KB).

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
cd frontend
npm install
cp .env.local.example .env.local   # NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE, defaults to :8000
npm run dev

Visit http://localhost:3000. The home page opens on a recorded example, so it shows a full investigation without calling the API. Run it live starts a real one and streams it step by step; its id goes into the URL, so a reload replays the stored run. A real finding needs the backend running with a real SURVEILLANCE_OPENAI_API_KEY; against a placeholder key the run still streams but ultimately fails, exercising the error state honestly rather than faking one. The How we know it works page reads frontend/src/generated/rl-policies.json.

NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE and NEXT_PUBLIC_DOCS_URL are baked in at build time.

The generated files in frontend/src/generated/ (the example run and the RL results) are written by make eval and checked for drift in CI.

Types are generated from the FastAPI OpenAPI schema, never hand-written:

make frontend-types    # backend schema -> frontend/src/lib/api-types.ts

make frontend-e2e runs the Playwright smoke test (the recorded example, loading, success, reload replay, empty, error, a failed audit and the evaluation page) against a fully mocked backend, with no live LLM, network or Python process. make docs-screenshots captures every page and state in light and dark and fails on any console error.

An accession that is not in facts.db is rejected up front with 404 and an actionable detail; no run is created. Browser calls are allowed from SURVEILLANCE_FRONTEND_ORIGINS (default http://localhost:3000; in development any localhost port is also allowed). To put it on a server, see Deploy to a server.

docs.title: Data pipeline
docs.text: Filled in during Phase 1 — SEC EDGAR ingestion, the date-parsing fix, amendment supersession, and the seeded compliance database. See docs/PLAN.md §4.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

The system is a small pipeline: plan the investigation, check the plan makes sense, gather evidence with a fixed set of tools, draft a conclusion, check that conclusion against the evidence, and only then show it to you.

graph TD
  plan[plan] --> check_plan{check_plan}
  check_plan -- replan, max 1 --> plan
  check_plan -- ok --> investigate[investigate + tools]
  investigate --> draft[draft_finding]
  draft --> extract[extract_claims]
  extract --> judge{judge_grounding}
  judge -- unsupported --> investigate
  judge -- supported --> publish[publish]

See docs/PLAN.md §5 for the full design and the reasoning behind each decision. See Decisions for the six architecture decision records this build produced, each with the alternative it rejected and why.

docs.title: API and persistence
docs.text: POST /investigations starts one run as an in-process background task and returns immediately; GET /investigations/{id} and GET /investigations/{id}/events read from RunStore (SQLite, data/runs.db) — every node event, the terminal finding, and per-node LLM cost are persisted as the run executes, so a run is replayable from the store whether a client is watching live or reconnects after the fact. See api.md for the generated reference.

docs.title: The state object
docs.text:
SurveillanceState (src/surveillance/graph/state.py) is a TypedDict threaded through every node in the graph:

Field Type Purpose messages Annotated[Sequence[BaseMessage], add_messages] The investigator's conversation with the tool-calling model; append-only via LangGraph's add_messages reducer. accession_number str The SEC Form 4 filing under investigation. plan InvestigationPlan \| None The planner's proposed tool-call sequence. plan_check PlanCheck \| None Deterministic validation result for plan (never LLM-authored). replan_count int Bounded retry counter for the planning loop. started_at float Wall-clock start time, used for the budget guardrail. draft_finding ComplianceFinding \| None The investigator's conclusion, plus deterministically-derived exculpatory factors. claims list[Claim] The draft finding's finding_text decomposed into discrete, tool_call_id-cited claims. grounding_report GroundingReport \| None Per-claim judgments plus the deterministically-aggregated unsupported count and confidence. evidence_pass int Bounded retry counter for the grounding loop. published_finding PublishedFinding \| None The terminal artifact: the judged draft plus its grounding report, assembled with no model call.

create_initial_state(accession_number) builds the starting state for a run.

docs.title: Graph flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    plan[plan] --> check_plan[check_plan]
    check_plan -- ok --> investigate[investigate]
    check_plan -- incomplete, replan_count < 1 --> replan[replan]
    check_plan -- incomplete, replan_count exhausted --> investigate
    replan --> check_plan
    investigate -- tool_calls --> tools[tools]
    tools --> investigate
    investigate -- done --> draft_finding[draft_finding]
    investigate -- over budget --> budget_exceeded[budget_exceeded]
    draft_finding --> extract_claims[extract_claims]
    extract_claims --> judge_grounding[judge_grounding]
    judge_grounding -- unsupported, evidence_pass < 2 --> investigate
    judge_grounding -- supported, or evidence_pass exhausted --> publish[publish]
    publish --> END
    budget_exceeded --> END

docs.title: Three bounded loops
docs.text:
1. Planning loop (plan → check_plan → replan → check_plan → ...). check_plan is a deterministic node (check_plan.py) — it verifies the plan calls get_transaction_details first and covers every mandatory tool in MANDATORY_TOOLS. Per D-A2-2 ("plan once, validate in code"), only one LLM call produces the plan; validation and replanning-feedback text are both plain code. replan_count is capped at MAX_REPLANS = 1 (graph/edges.py) — after one failed replan, the graph proceeds to investigate anyway rather than looping forever.

  2. Investigation loop (investigate ⇄ tools). The investigator model requests tool calls, ToolNode executes them against the real SQLite stores, and results feed back into investigate. route_after_agent (graph/edges.py) checks the real default Budget (graph/budget.py, max_tool_calls=15, max_wall_clock_seconds=120.0) on every turn and routes to budget_exceeded — which emits an incomplete=True, disposition="escalate" finding — rather than letting the loop run away.

  3. Grounding loop (draft_finding → extract_claims → judge_grounding → back to investigate, or on to publish). See How it works → Grounding for the full design. evidence_pass is capped at MAX_EVIDENCE_PASSES = 2 (graph/edges.py) — once the cap is reached, the run publishes anyway rather than looping forever, with whatever stayed unsupported visible in the published grounding_report.

docs.title: Deterministic evidence, not model-authored
docs.text:
graph/evidence.py turns the raw AIMessage/ToolMessage pairs in messages into typed ToolCallRecords (extract_tool_call_records) and derives ExculpatoryFactors from them (derive_exculpatory_factors) — e.g. reported_under_10b5_1, tax_withholding (transaction code F), option_exercise (code M), and below_all_thresholds. This is deliberately code, not an LLM call: "don't spend a model call on a decision an if can make" (docs/PLAN.md). draft_finding.py attaches these factors to the LLM's narrative ComplianceFindingDraft to produce the final ComplianceFinding.

The same discipline applies to the grounding loop: judge_grounding.py's LLM call only scores each individual claim as supported or not; the unsupported count and the resulting confidence are computed afterwards in plain code, never authored by the model.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

The agent cannot invent facts. It can only call one of six fixed, deterministic lookups against real data — every answer it gives has to trace back to one of these calls.

Six tools, each wrapping a single, parameterised query — the agent cannot construct arbitrary SQL, and every tool result is addressable evidence the grounding judge can cite (see Grounding).

Tool Purpose Backing store get_transaction_details Every transaction line reported in one filing, plus filing/insider context FactStore get_applicable_role_limits The synthetic firm-policy limits that apply to a relationship/title — never asserts authorisation PolicyStore get_compliance_rules The full severity-tiered rule table PolicyStore rolling_90d_trading_volume An insider's trading volume in a rolling 90-day window ending at a given date, by transaction code FactStore insider_trading_baseline An insider's own trailing transaction-value distribution, anchored to a given date FactStore get_material_events Whether a date falls inside a seeded corporate-event blackout window PolicyStore

docs.title: Design decisions carried from docs/PLAN.md §3–§4
docs.text:
• get_transaction_details returns every line in the filing, not one row. A single accession can report a tax-withholding line and a sale together; returning only one would make it impossible for the grounding judge to catch an exemption bleeding from one line onto another (canonical scenario 7).
  • Every lookback is anchored to an explicit as_of_date, never now(). The source notebook compared against the current wall-clock time while investigating a fixed historical window, making its own lookback meaningless.
  • One store connection per process, injected via a factory (tools/registry.py), not reopened per call. build_tools(fact_store, policy_store) returns all six tools bound to shared store instances.
  • Naming does not overclaim. get_applicable_role_limits, not get_insider_authorization — see What it won't do.

Tested with no LLM and no network — see tests/tools/.

docs.title: ADR index
docs.text:
Architecture decision records for the trade surveillance agent, referenced from docs/PLAN.md §8. Each records a decision, the alternative it rejected, and why — not just what was built.

ID Decision D-A2-1 Publication is deterministic D-A2-2 Plan once, validate in code D-A2-3 No vector store D-A2-4 Fallback is for availability, not validation D-A2-5 The vocabulary does not overclaim D-A2-6 Two evaluation layers D-A2-7 The process audit is the reward's trajectory component D-A2-8 Reward design D-A2-9 Gymnasium is dev-only and confined to evals

docs.title: D-A2-1: Publication is deterministic
docs.text: Status: Accepted, implemented (graph/nodes/publish.py, Phase 4).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: An earlier design ran judge_grounding → finalizer, where the finalizer was a second LLM call that wrote the finding a user actually sees. Grounding checked the draft, but a fresh model call wrote the published text afterward — meaning a passing grounding check said nothing about the words that ultimately got published. An unsupported claim could be reintroduced after the check that was supposed to catch it. That defeats the point of grounding at all.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The draft is the artifact under judgement, and publication is a plain function, not a model call:

draft_finding (LLM) → extract_claims (LLM, decomposes the draft's own text)
                    → judge_grounding (LLM, scores each claim)
                    → publish (no model call)

publish builds PublishedFinding from the judged draft's own model_dump() plus the grounding report — it cannot alter finding_text because it never sees a prompt. A test (tests/graph/test_publish.py::test_publish_is_byte_identical_to_the_judged_draft, plus the end-to-end version in tests/graph/test_surveillance_graph_integration.py) asserts published.finding_text == draft_finding.finding_text on every CI run.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The published finding is provably the same text that was judged — not regenerated, not summarized, not re-worded.
  • On a grounding failure, the entire draft is discarded and the investigation returns to investigate with specific unsupported-claim feedback (docs/PLAN.md §5.1) — there is no path to "patch" a bad draft into a passing one without re-investigating.
  • One fewer LLM call per investigation than the rejected design (no finalizer), which also lowers cost and latency.

docs.title: D-A2-2 Plan once, validate in code
D-A2-2: Plan once, validate in code
docs.text: Status: Accepted, implemented (graph/nodes/{plan,check_plan,replan}.py, Phase 3).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The investigation has a small, mostly-fixed set of six tools and a known checklist of mandatory evidence (transaction details first, then role limits, compliance rules, rolling volume, baseline, material events). An LLM planner plus an LLM critic plus several replan attempts burns multiple model calls validating something a plain function can check exactly: whether a plan references real tools, in the right order, covering the required checks.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
plan is exactly one LLM call. check_plan is deterministic code — it verifies the plan calls get_transaction_details first and covers every tool in MANDATORY_TOOLS, producing a PlanCheck(ok, missing_checks, unknown_tools, ordering_issues) that is never model-authored. replan is capped at one attempt (MAX_REPLANS = 1, graph/edges.py); if the plan is still imperfect after that, the graph proceeds to investigate anyway with the remaining issues visible in plan_check, rather than deadlocking.

The same "don't spend a model call on a decision an if can make" argument recurs twice more in this codebase: graph/evidence.py's exculpatory-factor derivation and graph/judge_grounding.py's unsupported/confidence aggregation are both deterministic for the same reason.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One planning LLM call per investigation instead of the several a planner-plus-critic-plus-retries design would need.
  • check_plan's correctness is testable exactly, with plain unit tests (tests/graph/test_check_plan.py) — no flakiness from a second model's judgement of the first model's plan.
  • The replan cap means a persistently bad plan is visible (in plan_check) rather than silently retried forever or blocking the run.

docs.title: D-A2-3: No vector store
docs.text: Status: Accepted, implemented (store/policy_store.py, tools/get_compliance_rules.py).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The portfolio-wide toolchain standard favors a vector store (Qdrant) for retrieval. This project's evidence, though, is not unstructured text to search semantically — it is a small, exact table of role limits, compliance-rule thresholds, and a corporate-events calendar. There is no genuine retrieval problem: every query the agent needs ("what's the single-trade limit for this role", "which rules apply", "is this date in a blackout window") has one exact, correct answer in SQL, not a ranked list of approximately-relevant passages.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Compliance rules, role limits, and material events live in SQLite (policy.db, data/generate_compliance_db.py), queried by exact key through typed tool functions (get_applicable_role_limits, get_compliance_rules, get_material_events). No embeddings, no similarity search, no vector database anywhere in this repo.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A rule citation (rule_id) is always exact and traceable to a specific row, never an approximate match that might retrieve the wrong rule.
  • No embedding-model dependency, no reindexing pipeline, no vector-store infrastructure to run, monitor, or pay for.
  • This is a deliberate exception to the portfolio-wide "Qdrant everywhere" toolchain default (PORTFOLIO_PLAN_V3.md §9) — the default is for apps with a genuine unstructured-retrieval problem, and stating the exception explicitly is more useful than following the default reflexively.

docs.title: D-A2-4: Fallback is for availability, not validation
docs.text: Status: Partially implemented. Single-provider profile (OpenAI) ships in base; the Gemini availability-fallback and Ollama offline profile described below are designed but not yet built (graph/policies.py module docstring tracks this explicitly).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A common but dangerous pattern is to catch any exception from a model call and retry against a different provider. That silently papers over the exact class of failure this app exists to surface — a schema-validation failure or a tool-calling defect is a real problem with the prompt or the model, not a transient availability issue, and hiding it behind an automatic fallback means a broken investigation can look like a successful one.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Fallback exists to handle transport-level failure only — connection errors, timeouts, 429s, 5xxs — never to catch and retry past a schema or tool-calling failure, which must surface as a real error. The planned design: OpenAI as the primary provider; a Gemini equivalent engages only on transport-level failure; an explicit offline profile (Ollama, selected by a setting, not engaged automatically) for local development and a data-sovereignty demo. .with_structured_output() must be bound per model before composing any fallback wrapper — calling it on an already-fallback-wrapped runnable does not behave correctly.

Base (Phases 3–7) ships only the OpenAI profile (build_fast_model/build_reasoning_model, graph/policies.py). The Gemini fallback and Ollama offline profile, and the cross-provider contract tests that would run outside pull-request CI against the same Pydantic schemas, are scheduled but not blocking the base build.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Today: a transport failure surfaces as a run failure (RunStore.fail_run), not a silent retry — honest, if less resilient than the target design.
  • When built: an outage of one provider doesn't take the whole app down, but a genuine schema or tool-calling defect still surfaces immediately rather than being masked by a fallback attempt.
  • Deferring this was a deliberate scope decision, not an oversight — it does not block anything in the base build's exit criteria, and building it before the base pipeline was proven end to end would have been premature.

docs.title: D-A2-5: The vocabulary does not overclaim
docs.text: Status: Accepted, implemented throughout tools/, schemas/, graph/evidence.py.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The source material this project's problem framing drew on used names that assert more than the evidence supports: get_insider_authorization implies a trade was cleared; "valid 10b5-1 plan" implies verification that never happened; an exculpatory factor derived from one transaction line could silently be read as clearing the whole filing.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Every name and value in this codebase is scoped to exactly what the evidence supports, nothing more:

  • get_applicable_role_limits, not get_insider_authorization — this tool selects an applicable limit from a seeded policy table; it does not assert that any trade was authorized or pre-cleared (tools/get_applicable_role_limits.py).
  • reported_under_10b5_1, not "valid 10b5-1 plan" — a tri-state (true/false/unknown) reflecting only whether the filing reported the indicator, never whether a plan was independently verified. unknown renders in the UI as "not established" — never as an absence of a plan (frontend/src/components/EvidencePanel.tsx).
  • ExculpatoryFactor.applies_to_transaction_sk scopes every exemption to one transaction line, never a whole accession — a tax-withholding line's exemption must never be read as clearing an unrelated sale in the same filing (canonical scenario 7, graph/evidence.py).
  • pre_cleared is deliberately absent from ExculpatoryKind — there is no approvals-workflow evidence anywhere in this system to support it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A reviewer reading a published finding cannot mistake a data-lookup result for a compliance conclusion the system doesn't have evidence for.
  • Renaming cost nothing at build time (these are new names on a from-scratch implementation, not a rename of shipped code) but would be expensive to retrofit after a name had shipped and been relied upon.
  • This discipline is enforced at the type level where possible (ExculpatoryKind's Literal has no pre_cleared member to accidentally reach for) rather than by convention alone.

docs.title: D-A2-6: Two evaluation layers
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Layer 1 implemented (evals/, Phase 7). Layer 2 designed, not populated — see Evaluation.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Ten hand-designed scenarios are enough to smoke-test behavior, but not enough to publish a precision or recall figure — one wrong case would move such a number by ten points, and live model output varies run to run. Conflating "does the mechanism work" with "how good is it in general" is exactly the kind of unlabelled claim this project exists to argue against.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Two layers, never conflated:

  • Layer 1 — canonical regression set (data/scenarios.py, n=10). Deterministic, fast, gates every pull request (make eval, .github/workflows/ci.yml). These are smoke tests for behavior, not a measurement — the metrics they produce (evals/metrics.py) are reported with n=10 and a clear "canonical, not stratified" label everywhere they appear (docs/evidence/evaluation.md).
  • Layer 2 — stratified evaluation set (150–300 cases, sampled across transaction code, relationship, value decile, 10b5-1 status, and amendment status; hand-labelled; run against pinned model versions on a schedule or manual trigger). Every number this layer produces states sample size, label source, model version, run date, and a confidence interval.

evals/metrics.py's compute_metrics() is shared by both layers, so neither layer re-derives a metric definition ad hoc.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Layer 1 catches a real regression class immediately and cheaply (it found two scenario-authoring bugs during Phase 7 — see Evaluation) without needing a live model or human labelling effort.
  • Layer 2 does not exist yet in this environment: no live LLM API key and no human labelling effort were available in this build. Rather than fabricate a placeholder precision number, docs/evidence/evaluation.md states this plainly. The harness (evals/metrics.py) is ready for it.
  • No number appears anywhere in this project's docs without stating what it is based on.

docs.title: D-A2-7: The process audit is the reward's trajectory component
docs.text: Status: Accepted, implemented in graph/trajectory_audit.py and attached by graph/nodes/publish.py.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The product checks the plan (check_plan) and, through an LLM judge, whether each claim is supported. Nothing deterministic checks what the investigator actually did: whether it gathered every required piece of evidence, started with the transaction details, cited only tool calls that exist, or stated an exemption the filing does not back.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
One pure function, audit_trajectory, inspects the tool-call records, the claims and the claimed exemptions, and returns a ProcessAudit. It lives in src/ so the product and the later RL reward share a single implementation.

  • publish attaches the audit to PublishedFinding.process_audit. It is record-only: it never changes the disposition, the text or the routing, so "published == judged draft" (D-A2-1) still holds.
  • below_all_thresholds is never an exemption. Being under the dollar limits says nothing about a blackout or late-filing violation.
  • An exemption naming a transaction must hold for that line; a tax-withholding F line does not support an exemption on an unrelated S line (canonical case 7).
  • No claims scores citation_validity = 0, not a vacuous 1: nothing is traceable.
  • Exemptions asserted in claim text are found with a keyword map. A clause containing a negation ("no 10b5-1 plan was reported", "status unknown") is skipped.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Exculpatory factors are derived from tool results in code, so the structured field is valid by construction. The audit's value in the product is the narrative mention, the citation check and the coverage check.
  • The negation rule under-detects rather than over-detects: a clause such as "although unproven, this was a 10b5-1 sale" is not caught. A false alarm on a correctly negated sentence was judged worse than a miss, because the audit is shown to reviewers.
  • Budget-exceeded runs end at budget_exceeded without publishing, so they carry no audit.

docs.title: D-A2-8: Reward design
docs.text: Status: Accepted, implemented in evals/rl_env.py (compute_reward).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The RL environment needs a reward. The obvious choice, scoring the submitted disposition against the label, is the same outcome-only scoring that lets always_flag reach 100% flag recall. And any reward built on a trajectory score has a trap: scaling a wrong answer by it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
An outcome table, a trajectory multiplier applied only to positive outcomes, unscaled penalties, and no LLM judge.

Expected, then submitted Outcome correct +1.0 clear, then flag -0.25 clear, then escalate -0.50 flag, then clear -0.75 flag, then escalate -0.10 escalate, then flag -0.25 escalate, then clear -1.0
  • Missing a violation is worse than over-alerting. A severity miss (flag versus escalate) is milder than a wrong direction. Alert fatigue is the real cost of a false positive (False positives).
  • total = outcome x P when the outcome is positive, where P is the process audit's trajectory_score (D-A2-7). Otherwise total = outcome.
  • Then subtract 0.01 per tool call beyond the six mandatory ones and 0.05 per invalid action. Truncation by the budget is a flat -0.5.
  • The LLM grounding judge is not part of the reward. A persuasive claim must not raise a score, and the reward must stay deterministic.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• If a wrong answer were multiplied by P, an agent that skips all evidence (P = 0) would turn every wrong answer into 0. Whenever it was unsure, skipping evidence would beat investigating. test_penalties_are_never_scaled_by_the_trajectory_score pins this, and the gate's blind_always_clear check catches it end to end.
  • The reward is only as strong as the policies that probe it. Two deliberate bugs initially passed the gate; see RL environment.
  • A reference score of 1.00 is a consistency check, never a performance claim.

docs.title: D-A2-9: Gymnasium is dev-only and confined to evals
docs.text: Status: Accepted, enforced by an import-linter contract.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The RL environment subclasses gymnasium.Env. The surveillance product must not depend on it: a reviewer should be able to read, run and deploy the product with the RL layer removed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: gymnasium is in the dev extra only and is imported only under evals/. The import-linter contract "no DSPy, DeepEval or gymnasium outside evals/optimize" forbids the surveillance package from importing it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The production image does not install it.
  • The process audit, which the reward reuses, lives in src/ with no gymnasium import, so the dependency points one way: evals depends on surveillance, never the reverse.
  • Deleting evals/rl_*.py leaves the product and its tests intact.

docs.title: Cost and latency
docs.text:
In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

Every investigation has a real cost and a real time-to-answer, and both are tracked per run rather than estimated after the fact.

graph/cost_tracking.py's CostTrackingHandler attributes every LLM call's tokens and estimated cost to the LangGraph node that made it, using each call's langgraph_node run metadata — no manual threading through node code. RunStore (store/run_store.py) persists this per real API investigation run; the chart below instead comes from the Layer 1 canonical eval run (evals/canonical.py), the only run this environment can generate on demand.

Per-node latency, Layer 1 canonical run

Cost is $0 for every canonical scenario — an honest consequence of Layer 1 using evals/oracle.py's deterministic chains rather than a live model in this environment (see Evaluation), not a placeholder. The cost-tracking arithmetic itself is exercised directly against real LLMResult payloads in tests/graph/test_cost_tracking.py, and will show real per-node dollar figures the first time POST /investigations runs against a live model with SURVEILLANCE_OPENAI_API_KEY set — visible via GET /investigations/{id} and the UI cost meter (Phase 6).

Latency here is real: each canonical investigation's full graph run — planning, tool calls against the real SQLite stores, the grounding loop — timed end to end, p50/p95 computed the same way evals/metrics.py would for a live-model Layer 1 or Layer 2 run.

docs.title: Data profile
docs.text:
In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

Before writing any investigation logic, we looked at what the real SEC data actually contains. That look changed the design in several places — most importantly, it caught a bug in the original source material that would have made two of five tools silently useless.

Generated from a real, live fetch of three SEC EDGAR quarters (2025 Q4 – 2026 Q2), 273,482 transactions, via make docs-assets (docs/generate_plots.py). CI fails if regenerating these charts produces a diff, so they can never drift from the data they describe.

docs.title: Transaction codes are not just "buy" and "sell"
docs.text:
273,482 transactions, 2025 Q4 – 2026 Q2

F (tax withholding) and M (option exercise) are the third and fourth most common codes — more common than ordinary purchases. Both are routinely non-suspicious. A naive value-threshold rule would flag tens of thousands of these every quarter, which is exactly how a surveillance system gets switched off from alert fatigue. See docs/PLAN.md §3.3.8.

docs.title: Most sales are not made under a 10b5-1 plan
docs.text:
AFF10B5ONE distribution across the fetched dataset

The minority that are reported under a plan are the exculpatory cases this system must never flag.

docs.title: Filing lag against the Section 16(a) deadline
docs.text:
Section 16(a) filing lag, in NYSE trading days

Measured in NYSE trading days, not calendar days — the two diverge around exchange holidays, which is exactly where a generic business-day calendar would misjudge lateness.

docs.title: Transaction value by relationship
docs.text: Transaction value distribution by RPTOWNER_RELATIONSHIP

docs.title: Why three quarters of data, not one
docs.text:
Three fetched quarters vs. the single target quarter

A rolling 90-day volume check and a 180-day trading-history baseline both need real history behind the target quarter. Fetching only the target quarter would silently starve both checks for every transaction early in that quarter.

docs.title: A real data-quality finding
docs.text: The live fetch surfaced something the reference sample didn't: SEC's own disclaimer states filer-submitted data "cannot guarantee accuracy," and in practice roughly 0.4% of transaction dates in this dataset are implausible (e.g. a year typo shifting a date by decades, or into the future). This is a known EDGAR data-quality limitation, not a bug in this pipeline — the zero-null-date assertion catches unparseable dates; implausible-but-parseable dates are a distinct problem, tracked for a future plausibility-bound filter rather than blocking Phase 1.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

Every published number here states how many cases it's based on, where the labels came from, and what model version produced it — a claim without that context is exactly what this project exists to argue against.

docs.title: Layer 1 — canonical regression set (n=10)
docs.text:
make eval (evals/run.py) runs all 10 scenarios from data/scenarios.py through the real compiled graph — real nodes, real tools, real SQLite stores — and gates pull-request CI (.github/workflows/ci.yml) on an exact disposition match.

This environment has no LLM API key, so Layer 1 cannot use recorded live model responses. evals/oracle.py substitutes a deterministic, rules-based decision function — a reference oracle applying the same objective thresholds (single-trade limit, rolling 90-day limit, blackout window, filing lateness) a compliance officer would check, built from the same real tool outputs and the same deterministic exculpatory-factor logic (graph/evidence.py) the real graph uses. It is not a claim about LLM reasoning quality — it exercises the pipeline's plumbing (planning, tool wiring, evidence derivation, the grounding loop, publication) against a known-correct answer. evals/record_responses.py, capturing real transcripts once a live LLM is available, would replace it without changing evals/metrics.py or the CI gate.

docs.text: Not populated. A published precision/recall figure needs a hand-labelled, stratified sample (150–300 cases) graded against pinned model versions — this requires both a live LLM and real human labelling effort, neither of which this environment has. The harness this layer needs (evals/metrics.py, the same compute_metrics() Layer 1 already uses) is ready; nothing here fabricates a placeholder number in its absence, per the standard this project holds everyone else to.

docs.title: False positives
docs.text:
In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

The number that matters most to whether anyone would actually use this is how often it cries wolf on a clean trade — that's tracked explicitly here, not folded into a single accuracy number that could hide it.

Per Evaluation, the Layer 1 canonical run (n=10, oracle-scored) currently shows a 0% false-positive rate on clear labels — no clean trade in the canonical set was flagged or escalated. At n=10 this demonstrates the mechanism works, not a production false-positive rate; that number can only be published from Layer 2's stratified, hand-labelled set (150–300 cases) against pinned model versions, which does not exist yet (see Evaluation § Layer 2).

The alert-fatigue chart (precision/recall vs. alert volume) is not published for the same reason. It needs a labelled set large and varied enough to sweep a confidence threshold meaningfully — with 10 canonical cases, that curve would have three or four points and imply a precision this app exists to argue should never be published without an n beside it. This page will carry the real curve once Layer 2 is populated.

docs.title: RL environment: can a shortcut score well?
docs.text:
In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

The product investigates a trade and publishes a finding. This page asks a harder question: could an investigator that cuts corners still look good? To find out, the same investigation loop is turned into a small practice environment with a scoring rule, and a handful of scripted shortcut strategies are run through it. Each one scores far below a proper investigation, and a test in CI keeps it that way. It is an extra on top of the surveillance product, not the product itself.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
An insider-trading investigator can look right while cutting corners: skipping evidence, citing things it never retrieved, or asserting a 10b5-1 exemption the filing does not support. Wrong dispositions also have asymmetric costs: a missed violation is worse than an extra alert, but alert fatigue is the real price of over-flagging (False positives).

Regulatory frame: SEC Rule 10b-5, Section 16(a), Rule 10b5-1 and FINRA 3110 (see Regulatory basis).

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
What is checked, and by what:

Check By Where The plan covers every mandatory tool, details first Code check_plan Exculpatory factors come from tool results Code graph/evidence.py Each claim is supported by the evidence An LLM judge judge_grounding Evidence gathered, ordering, real citations, supported exemptions Code graph/trajectory_audit.py The reward Code, no LLM evals/rl_env.py

The process audit runs on every real investigation and is shown on the finding, record-only (D-A2-7). The reward reuses the same function as its trajectory component (D-A2-8).

docs.title: The environment
docs.text:
SurveillanceEnv is a Gymnasium environment. Observations and actions are JSON strings, which is what an LLM policy would emit.

  • reset returns the accession number, the tool list with argument schemas and the tool-call budget. It never returns a label, scenario id or name.
  • step takes either a tool call (the real tool runs) or a submit with a disposition, claims that cite tool-call ids, and any exemptions claimed.
  • Unparseable actions, unknown tools and bad arguments cost 0.05 and count toward the budget. Exceeding the budget ends the episode at -0.5.
  • Only the six real tools run; the plan, judge and finding nodes do not.

The reference reaching 1.00 on all ten scenarios is a consistency check of the environment and reward. The reference reuses the oracle's decision logic and the scenario labels were designed to match it, so it is not a performance claim. The informative column is the other one: every shortcut loses, and each loses for a specific reason.

docs.title: Gate
docs.text:
make eval runs the canonical eval and then evals/run_rl.py, in CI on every pull request. It fails if any of these is false:

  • the reference mean is exactly 1.00 and every reference episode ends in a submit;
  • every other policy scores at least 0.5 below the reference;
  • skipping evidence never scores above gathering it for the same answers;
  • no observation contains a scenario id or name.

A further CI step fails if the generated results file differs from the committed one. The scorer is the scripted stand-in; no live-model number is gated.

docs.title: Live-model run (not gated)
docs.text:
The same ten scenarios were run once through the real graph with real models and scored with the same compute_reward (make eval-live, evals/live_run.py). It is not part of make eval and no CI check depends on it.

n 10 canonical scenarios Models gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 (plan, investigate, claims), gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (finding, judge) Run date 2026-10-29 Labels designed with the scenarios, as above Disposition accuracy 4 of 10 Mean reward -0.03 (outcome only: 0.09) Cost $0.43 in total, about $0.04 per investigation Mean latency 33.5 s per investigation Uncertainty none computed; n=10 supports no precision claim, and one run varies from the next

Per-scenario results and every transcript are in evals/recordings/live-2026-10-29/. Two things stand out.

  • The model missed three of the four flag cases by clearing them, which the outcome table penalises hardest. The accuracy figure says nothing about model quality in general: ten cases, one run, one prompt version.
  • The process audit scored 0 on five of ten runs, and for a real reason. In those five the claim extractor cited no tool-call ids at all, so the audit's citation check failed. The grounding judge also marked many claims unsupported (between 1 and 5 per run), and those findings were still published once the two evidence passes were spent, with the unsupported count visible. A record-only audit and a judge that sees only the claims it is given are doing different jobs; here the audit surfaced a weakness in the claim extractor that the grounding report alone did not.

The recorded transcripts are what a later replay harness would use to replace the scripted stand-in (evals/oracle.py) with real responses. That replacement is not built yet.

docs.title: Lessons learned
docs.text:
1. Outcome-only scoring rewards always_flag. It gets 100% flag recall while being wrong on six of ten cases.
  2. Scaling penalties by the trajectory score makes skipping evidence the best strategy when unsure. A wrong answer multiplied by zero is zero, which beats a thorough wrong answer. Penalties are therefore never scaled (D-A2-8).
  3. Harness-building already exposed two scenarios that were trivially passable (Evaluation). The RL gate applies the same discipline to the reward.
  4. The first version of the gate could not catch two deliberate bugs. Breaking the reward so penalties were scaled, or removing the fabricated-id check, both left the gate green: no policy gave a wrong answer without evidence, and the fabricator cited only ghost ids, which a weaker check also zeroes. Adding blind_always_clear and making the fabricator cite one real and one invented id fixed both, and each mutation now fails make eval. A gate that has never been seen to fail is not evidence.

docs.title: Grounding
docs.text:
In one paragraph, for a non-engineer

Before this system tells you its conclusion, it checks its own homework: every sentence in the draft finding is compared against the actual evidence it retrieved, and if a sentence isn't backed by anything real, the draft is thrown out and the investigation keeps digging — up to two extra tries.

docs.title: Why the draft is judged, not the final answer
docs.text:
An earlier design ran the grounding judge before a separate model wrote the finding a user actually sees — so a passing grounding check said nothing about the words that got published. That defeats the point of grounding at all. This system instead judges the finding text itself:

flowchart LR
    draft_finding[draft_finding] --> extract_claims[extract_claims]
    extract_claims --> judge_grounding[judge_grounding]
    judge_grounding -- unsupported --> investigate[investigate]
    judge_grounding -- supported --> publish[publish]
  1. draft_finding (LLM) writes a complete candidate finding from the evidence gathered so far.
  2. extract_claims (LLM) decomposes that exact draft's finding_text into discrete claims, each citing the tool_call_ids it believes support it — never inventing an id that wasn't actually called.
  3. judge_grounding (LLM, scored per claim) checks each claim against the real recorded tool results. The aggregate unsupported count and the resulting confidence are computed afterwards in plain code, not by the model — the judge scores claims, code counts them.
  4. On a failure, the draft is discarded and the run returns to investigate with the specific unsupported claims as feedback, not a generic retry — capped at two extra evidence-gathering passes (evidence_pass ≤ 2).
  5. publish contains no model call. It assembles the terminal PublishedFinding from the judged draft's own data plus the grounding report — so the text a user reads is provably the text that was judged, never rewritten afterward.

docs.title: Unsupported claims per grounding pass
docs.text:
Unsupported claim count falling across evidence passes

This chart is generated by actually running the production build_judge_grounding_node code (docs/generate_plots.py, grounding_loop_unsupported_claims()) through a scripted three-pass run — a real investigation whose evidence improves each pass, judged by the real deterministic aggregation logic. It uses a scripted stand-in for the live grounding-judge model, since this deployment has no LLM API key configured for chart generation; the mechanism it demonstrates — evidence_pass rising as unsupported claims fall, capped at 2 — is exactly what tests/graph/ test_surveillance_graph_integration.py exercises end to end against the real graph.

docs.title: What this catches, and what it doesn't
docs.text: Grounding checks that a claim is backed by a tool result the run actually retrieved — it does not re-verify that the tool result itself is correct, and it does not check the compliance conclusion is right, only that the sentence asserting it points at real evidence. A well-grounded finding can still be wrong if the underlying data or rule table is wrong; that is why every published finding carries a prototype disclaimer and a human stays in the loop (see Regulatory basis).

docs.title: In plain language
docs.text:
In one paragraph

Imagine a compliance officer who has to check whether an executive's stock sale was suspicious. They would look up who the person is, what they're allowed to trade, how much they've traded recently, and whether anything about the timing looks wrong. This system automates exactly that checklist over real SEC filings — and shows its work at every step, checking its own conclusion against the evidence before it tells you anything.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Executives, directors, and large shareholders have to publicly report their own stock trades within two business days. Regulators and compliance teams watch these reports for patterns that warrant a closer look — a sale timed suspiciously close to upcoming news, a trade far larger than someone normally makes, a filing that showed up late. Doing this by hand, for every filing, does not scale; doing it with an AI system that can quietly hallucinate a plausible-sounding but wrong conclusion is arguably worse than not doing it at all.

docs.title: What this system does about it
docs.text:
1. Plans which pieces of evidence it needs (who is this person, what are they allowed to trade, what rules apply, how does this compare to their own history, is there a blackout window) — checked by code, not trusted blindly.
  2. Investigates by calling real tools against real data — never inventing a fact it hasn't actually looked up.
  3. Drafts a conclusion, then decomposes that conclusion into individual claims and checks each one against the evidence it actually gathered — not the conversation, the evidence.
  4. If a claim isn't backed by anything real, the draft is thrown out and the investigation goes back to gather more evidence, up to two extra tries, before it's willing to publish anything.
  5. Only then does it publish — and the published text is provably the exact text that passed that check, never rewritten afterward.

docs.title: Why this matters more than the trading rules themselves
docs.text:
The insider-trading domain here is realistic, but it is a vehicle for the actual point: an AI system that can show, for any claim it makes, exactly which piece of real evidence backs it up — and that refuses to publish a claim it can't back. That pattern generalizes far beyond insider trading.

See How it works → Grounding for the mechanism, and What it won't do for this system's honest limits.

All of these states are tested by the same Playwright suite (frontend/e2e/investigation.spec.ts).

A run that can't be started. The API rejects an unknown accession with a 404 and an actionable message, which the page shows as is. A backend that is unreachable or over its rate limit shows a generic message. A run that failed, or was cut off by a server restart, shows its stored error.

docs.text:
The How we know it works page explains the RL environment and shows how each scripted shortcut scores. See RL environment.

docs.title: What it won't do
docs.text:
• It does not watch live trades or price feeds — it investigates transactions already reported to the SEC.
  • It does not decide anything on its own. Every finding is a research artifact for a human reviewer, never a supervisory action.
  • It does not use real firm policy — the trading-limit table is a synthetic seeded dataset, documented as such throughout.
  • It is not a medical, legal, or financial advice system, and it is not a system of record.

See regulatory basis for what it is grounded in.
